comment.value: This paper proposes DeepASA, which trains a single deep network to perform multiple audio scene analysis tasks, including source separation, dereverb, sound event detection, audio tagging, and direction-of-arrival estimation. This is realized by first separating the mixtures (Object-Oriented Processing strategy), creating hidden representations for each sound object, and then using various decoders on the hidden representations to estimate auditory parameters, with further refinement achieved by a Chain-of-Inference mechanism. Through extensive discussions the reviewers are happy with the method and results presented in this paper.

rebuttal.value:
**Weak-Q1.** DeepASA has significantly higher computational cost than DeFT-Mamba, the model it is based on despite often only achieving modest accuracy gains.

**A.** (1) Compared to DeFT-Mamba, DeepASA covers a wider range of tasks. It can perform separation, denoising, dereverberation, sound event detection, and DoA estimation for up to 5 sources. In the ASA2 dataset, it showed an improvement of 0.8 dB in SI-SDR and 0.7 dB in SDR compared to DeFT-Mamba.

(2) When only performing USS, DeepASA has a lower computational load but higher performance than DeFT-Mamba. Initially, we incorrectly reported the computational cost on the MC-FUSS dataset. In the MC-FUSS dataset, only the audio decoder is used, and the other decoders are not utilized, which reduces the parameter size and computational complexity of DeepASA. 
To ensure a fair comparison with DeFT-Mamba, we compared the performance of DeepASA trained from scratch on the MC-FUSS dataset without using the pre-trained ATST with the performance in Table 3. The experimental results are as follows: DeepASA without using a pre-trained ATST has a lower parameter size and computational complexity than DeFT-Mamba, but its performace improved for all source counts, even when it is trained from scratch. This is attributed to the exclusion of F-Mamba, which improves sound separation performance but has a high computational load, and the introduction of the proposed dynamic STFT and noise decoder. We will add these experimental results to the main paper.

**Weak-Q2.** Chain-of-inference is defined as one of the two major contributions of the paper. But the results do not seem to warrant this focus. In fact, the biggest improvements over previous models can be seen in the MC-FUSS dataset where chain-of-inference is not even used at all.

**A.** The improvement on the MC-FUSS dataset is due to the comprehensive object separation and analysis introduced in deepASA. These include dereverberation, multichannel-to-multichannel (M2M) separation, dynamic STFT process, and noise estimation. These modifications brought the biggest improvements when only the USS task was performed. However, the improvement on the USS task does not mean the inefficacy of the chain-of-inference (CoI). In our ablation study with and without CoI, the model with CoI demonstrates +0.3 dB in the SDRi and -0.024 in a SELD score, compared to the model without CoI in the ASA2 dataset. Additionally, the model is able to surpass the existing models by using CoI in the STARSS23 dataset.

Additionally, we applied the CoI to existing SELD models and observed performance improvements. Existing models do not employ object-oriented processing, so only the cross-attention from temporal coherence matching was applied to the existing models. The experimental results are shown in the table below, and since both models exhibited similar enhancements, this demonstrates the generalizability of CoI.

**Weak-Q3.** Other than the MC-FUSS, the accuracy improvements of the DeepASA over previous work are more modest, a combination of many minor improvements adding up.

**A.**
- In terms of performance, the benchmark for the STARSS23 dataset in Table 4 of the DCASE challenge permitted the use of pre-trained models and external large datasets, as well as data augmentation, resulting in each system using different training data and pre-trained models. Consequently, in Table 8 of the Appendix, the performance of SOTA models for the sound event localization and detection (SELD) task without the use of external data or data augmentation is listed. The comparison with the performance of DeepASA without using the pre-trained ATST can be found in the reply to the previous comment (Weak-Q1-A). Ultimately, DeepASA achieved a 0.6 dB improvement over the best performance of previous works in terms of SI-SDRi and a 0.141 improvement in SELD score compared to the best performance of previous works in a fair comparison. This can be considered a sufficiently significant gap.
- Also, the main contribution of DeepASA is not its exceptionally high performance on a specific task but rather its ability to enhance performance across various tasks by learning multiple auditory information (class, timestamp, and DoA) through several sub-decoders to separate object features. In other words, DeepASA contributes not only in terms of model architecture but also in its training methodology. From a model structure perspective, it improves efficiency by excluding the computationally intensive F-Mamba and allows for the learning of time resolution and frequency lobes over time through dynamic STFT. Additionally, it enhances the estimation performance of individual auditory information through cross-referencing multiple auditory information sources, similar to human processing. The DeepASA and chain-of-inference structure is a novel architecture not previously proposed.

**Question-Q1.** In lines 307-308 you write "This performance gain is largely attributed to the noise decoder’s explicit estimation of background noise and the benefits of fine-tuning from pre-trained weights."

**A.** Estimating background noise is essential because, when only the foreground source is separated, noise often mixes into the inactive source, which should be estimated as silence. To prevent this, noise separation is explicitly learned. A similar approach based on loss functions has existed in speech enhancement [**]. Specifically, by estimating noise, the sum of the foreground source and noise is constrained to be the audio mixture, which indirectly constrains the phase of the estimated foreground sources. This helps reduce artifacts that occur when using loss in the STFT domain. This approach also contributes to improving classification performance in this paper.

[**] A. Pandey, D.L. Wang, "Dense CNN with self-attention for time-domain speech enhancement." IEEE/ACM Trans. Audio, Speech, Lang. Process., 29, pp. 1270 – 1279, 2021.

**Question-Q2.** Figure 2 shows how the channel dimension is increased from 2M to D but the text (line 114) claims it increases from 2M to C. Is that just a mistake, given that C is later (line 162) defined as the number of classes?

**A.** Thank you for the reviewer’s comment. We defined C as the number of classes, and it needs to be D. We will change “from 2M to C” into “from 2M to D.”

**Paper Formatting Concerns.** This is a minor nitpick, but many metrics are only named by their abbreviations (SI-SDRi, SDRi, SA-SDR) and should be defined the first time they are named, e.g. scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio improvement (SI-SDRi), etc. The same is true for D, T' and C Figure 2. It is not immediately obvious what they are supposed to be from the Figure alone. The description of Table 3 should also mention it is the SI-SDRi in dB which is reported.

**A.** Thank you for pointing that out. We will define the first time the evaluation metrics are named. (scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio improvement (SI-SDRi), signal-to-distortion ratio (SDR), source-aggregated signal-to-distortion ratio (SA-SDR). As the reviewer commented, we will define D, T’, and C in the caption of Figure 2. We will mention that SI-SDRi is reported on the dB scale.

**Weak-Q1.** Figures 2 & 5 (model diagram & CoI) are dense and lack intuitive legends. Readers may struggle to follow data flow. I think a step-by-step schematic or callouts would help.

**A.** Thank you for pointing this out. We will revise the figures by creating a step-by-step schematic and adding detailed explanations in the captions so that the model structure can be understood just by looking at the figures. Specifically, in Figure 2, we aim to highlight how each object is processed in parallel on a batch basis through the object splitter. In Figure 5, we will clarify the signal flow from the SED and DoA query branches to TCM in the chain-of-inference. 


**Weak-Q2.** Dynamic STFT (Sec. 2.2) is novel but under-explained: it would be clearer with visualizations of learned windows over time and ablations on σₜ initialization.

**A.** Thank you for mentioning the dynamic STFT. We briefly introduced its ablation study and the visualization of the learned window (changes in standard deviation over time) in Appendix D, but as per the reviewer's suggestion, we will provide a more detailed visualization in the revised paper. First, we will add visualizations of the learned window (mean and standard deviation) from various samples. To summarize the results here, the mean slightly alters around zero for most samples, but the standard deviation (width of window) dynamically changes, indicating that the dynamic STFT is utilized for adjusting the temporal and spectral resolution.
- The ablation study on initialization of $\sigma_t$ shows that proper initialization is important. If $\sigma_t$ is not initialized with a size comparable to the width of the STFT analysis window, e.g., zero initialization, the features after the encoder do not sufficiently contain the information of the audio mixture, and the subsequent parameters cannot be trained for each task. Therefore, initialization is an essential element for learning, and as mentioned in the main text, $\sigma_t$ was set to 6.67 ms to ensure that $6\sigma_t$ can cover one frame.


**Weak-Q3.** The choice of maximum object count J is not justified: how sensitive is performance if fewer/more sources appear?

**A.** We set J=5 because the minimum maximum number of sources that allows the pre-trained model to be fine-tuned on the STARSS23 dataset is 5.
 We performed inference when the number of sound sources is within the maximum estimable range (S=2–5<=J) and when it exceeded the maximum estimable range (S=6–7>J). When the number of foreground sources is 6 or 7, resulting in a sharp decline in performance. The experimental results show that when there are 6 sources, two sources are not separated, leading to very low performance only for the two sources. When there are 7 sources, three sources are mixed and mapped to one track in most cases, resulting in very low performance for three of the sources.

**Weak-Q4.** Computational cost of the ATST-based SED decoder is high. It would be great to discuss the runtime and efficiency trade-offs.

**A.** We additionally compared the performance of the final DeepASA model without the pre-trained ATST on the ASA2 dataset and the MC-FUSS dataset. The experimental results showed that while the parameter size significantly decreased, the model's performance did not change significantly, and the reduced performance still surpassed other existing state-of-the-art models. **Weak-Q5.** Related Work (Sec. 5) omits object-centric learning: key works like "Slot Attention" (Locatello et al., 2020), "Sound of Pixels" (Zhao et al., 2018), "Objects That Sound" (Arandjelović et al., 2017), "SSV2A" (Guo et al., 2024), "AVObject" (Li et al., 2025), are not discussed. The distinction between those and DeepASA’s OOP should be clarified.

**A.** [Slot Attention] The key difference is that Slot Attention sets the slots first and then trains the mapping of objects to these slots, whereas OOP learns the spatial, frequency, and temporal relationships of the mixture audio first and then separates the objects through an object splitter. 

 The main difference between these works and the proposed OOP is that, unlike OOP’s core characteristic, these works do not process the separated features in parallel by permuting them along the batch dimension for each task (localization, separation, retrieval, and audio generation). In OOP, features are separated by the object splitter and processed independently in the batch dimension, fundamentally preventing interference from other object features.

 [Sound of Pixels] is a network that separates audio occurring at specific pixels on a pixel-level basis. It extracts video features through a video analysis network and audio features through an audio analysis network and then performs source separation in an audio synthesis network. This approach is similar to conventional audio source separation networks, which extract information for source separation and ultimately perform the separation.

 [Object that Sounds] proposes a network that fuses video and audio features for cross-modal retrieval, enabling semantic object localization. Similar to the previous Sound of Pixels, it utilizes object-centric learning. If OOP were applied to this work, features could be extracted through AVEnet, and the object splitter would separate each audio feature, allowing parallel retrieval of each sound source at the batch level.

 [SSV2A, AVObject] also employ object-centric learning in the multi-modal domain, similar to the previous two papers. In conclusion, the key difference between object-centric learning and OOP lies in whether objects are explicitly separated and then processed in parallel through a parameter-shared decoder by passing them as batches.


**Limitation-Q1.** The authors discuss the ATST size but could further elaborate on dataset biases (e.g., reverberation conditions) and potential misuses (e.g., surveillance).

**A.** Thank you for the suggestion. Additionally, because the background noise was simulated with an SNR range of 6 to 30 dB, the model’s performance is also expected to decline when the background noise has an SNR below 0 dB and is louder than the foreground source.

Next, regarding the potential misuse, since this model can extract individual speakers’ speech and analyze their types and directions, there is a concern that it could be exploited for eavesdropping.

summary.value:
This paper proposes DeepASA, which trains a single deep neural network (DNN) to do source separation, dereverb, sound event detection, audio tagging, and direction-of-arrival (DOA) estimation.

This is realized by first implicitly separating the mixtures, creating hidden representations for each sound object, and then using various decoders on the hidden representations to estimate auditory parameters such as sound event and DOA.

Evaluation results on their own customized training and test dataset (i.e., ASA2) and two public datasets (MC-FUSS and STARSS23) show that the proposed method can produce strong performance for sound separation and auditory parameter estimation.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:

DeepASA can simultaneously deal with multiple tasks, and obtains reasonable improvement over existing methods.

Weaknesses:

1.	Title, “one-for-all” is not accurate, as auditory scene analysis contains many more tasks, while DeepASA only addresses a subset of them. In addition, the considered combination of tasks is not so novel, as compared with existing SELD tasks (which already deal with SED, audio tagging and DOA estimation simultaneously), DeepASA only introduces separation.

2.	The evaluation is only performed on simulated datasets, and lacks convincing evaluation results on real-recorded datasets for sound separation. On real-recorded data, sound separation is usually difficult, as real data often mismatches simulated data. In this case, would the method still perform well, considering that the method relies so much on obtaining good hidden representations for each sound object (i.e., if the hidden representations for each sound object is not good on, e.g., real-recorded data, then auditory parameter estimation would be also not good)?

3.	Section 2.2, better to use “analysis window” to replace the word “window”, as “window” is overloaded with many meanings in signal processing.

4.	“SED decoder” in Section 2.4 and Figure 4(b) feel messy and are difficult to follow. The writing needs improvement.

5.	Many details are missing regarding the model. See my detailed questions to the authors.

6.	The comparison with existing models in Table 3 and 4 are not so fair, as they are trained on different sets of data, and DeepASA uses the ATST model (which is pre-trained on a very large dataset). It might not be surprising that DeepASA can obtain better performance. See also my detailed questions.

summary.value: Authors present DeepASA as a unified framework for acoustic scene analysis, adopting an Object-Oriented Processing approach that separates object-centric features at an early stage to avoid permutation ambiguity, and the Chain-of-Inference mechanism that iteratively refines predictions using temporal coherence matching between different auditory cues

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths
This paper addresses a fundamental challenge of comprehensive scene analysis, maintaining consistent object-wise associations across all sub-decoders task heads, as opposed to prior track0wise processing systems.

The motivation for object separator, CoI, as well as dynamic stft is clearly articulated and supported by ablation evidence. Temporal coherence matching is also shown to provide measurable improvements.

Weakness:
The overall model, even with pre-trained AST is notably bulky compared to task-specific approaches and is a concern for practical deployment. Additionally, given the multistage training, can authors provide an analysis of training convergence properties and sensitivity to initialization. Are there convergence guarantees for the chain-of-inference mechanism? I believe the 97M AST limits the novelty for SED component + is a computational bottleneck.

With regards to ASA2 dataset, the balanced distribution proportional to source count and increased maximum sources from 4 → 5 compared to prior versions suggests substantial modifications that could favor the proposed approach. Overall paper can benefit from highlighting some potential biases in ASA2

Foreground sources are fixed to J=5, however, some analysis regarding possible performance degradation when this assumption is violated would be helpful. Some analysis varying the degree of polyphonicity is expected. What is the computational and memory scaling behaviour?

Minor weakness:
The relationship between different loss components and their relative weighting could be better motivated in the main paper than in the appendix.

questions.value:
Could authors provide evidence for true object correspondence? .. some validation that object features actually correspond to individual sound sources rather than just being abstract encoded representations.

Is it possible to show that each of the J=5 object features consistently tracks the same sound source across time? When sounding objects enter and exit a scene, are object features able to maintain semantic coherence?

summary.value: This paper presents DeepASA, a unified framework for auditory scene analysis that performs multichannel source separation, dereverberation, sound event detection, audio classification, and direction-of-arrival estimation in one model. The core contributions are: (1) an Object-Oriented Processing (OOP) strategy, which isolates per-object audio features early in the pipeline via a transformer-based aggregator and object separator, and (2) a Chain-of-Inference (CoI) mechanism that iteratively refines object features by fusing sub-decoder outputs through temporal-coherence attention. Evaluated on three benchmarks (ASA2, MC-FUSS, STARSS23), DeepASA achieves state-of-the-art performance across all tasks.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths:
1. Ablations isolate each module’s contribution; end-to-end performance on multiple datasets is compelling.
2. Real-world examples on the demo webpage lend practical credibility.
3. Well-designed multi-decoder architecture eliminates permutation issues and enables complementary cue integration.

Weaknesses:
1. Figures 2 & 5 (model diagram & CoI) are dense and lack intuitive legends. Readers may struggle to follow data flow. I think a step-by-step schematic or callouts would help.
2. Dynamic STFT (Sec. 2.2) is novel but under-explained: it would be clearer with visualizations of learned windows over time and ablations on σₜ initialization.
3. The choice of maximum object count J is not justified: how sensitive is performance if fewer/more sources appear?
4. Computational cost of the ATST-based SED decoder is high. It would be great to discuss the runtime and efficiency trade-offs.
5. Related Work (Sec. 5) omits object-centric learning: key works like "Slot Attention" (Locatello et al., 2020), "Sound of Pixels" (Zhao et al., 2018), "Objects That Sound" (Arandjelović et al., 2017), "SSV2A" (Guo et al., 2024), "AVObject" (Li et al., 2025), are not discussed. The distinction between those and DeepASA’s OOP should be clarified.

limitations.value: The authors discuss the ATST size but could further elaborate on dataset biases (e.g., reverberation conditions) and potential misuses (e.g., surveillance).

final_justification.value: The paper contributes a unified framework for auditory scene analysis. The experiments demonstrate its effectiveness. After reading other reviewers' comments, I would like to recommend Borderline Accept.

summary.value:
The paper proposes DeepASA, a new model for auditory scene analysis, taking in a multichannel audio mixture capable of performing source separation, sount event detection, audio classification and direction-of-arrival estimation. The DeepASA model itself is based on the DeFT-Mamba model.
The two core contributions are the chain-of-inference architecture and object oriented processing.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strengths
- DeepASA is capable of performing universal sound separation, sound event detection and direction-of-arrival estimation all within one model 
- DeepASA outperforms previous models in most metrics on the three datasets it was tested on
- The proposed model is significantly more accurate with more than two foreground sources compared to the previous work on the MC-FUSS dataset
- Detailed ablation study was done for all the proposed changes


Weaknesses
- DeepASA has significantly higher computational cost than DeFT-Mamba, the model it is based on despite often only achieving modest accuracy gains.
- Chain-of-inference is defined as one of the two major contributions of the paper. But the results do not seem to warrant this focus. In fact, the biggest improvements over previous models can be seen in the MC-FUSS dataset where chain-of-inference is not even used at all.
- Other than the MC-FUSS, the accuracy improvements of the DeepASA over previous work are more modest, a combination of many minor improvements adding up.

questions.value:
1. In lines 307-308 you write 
>This performance gain is largely attributed to the noise decoder’s explicit estimation of background noise and the benefits of fine-tuning from pre-trained weights.

This is something I've wondered about when I saw Figure 2; why exactly is background noise estimated and how would it contribute to an improvement in estimating the foreground sources?

2. Figure 2 shows how the channel dimension is increased from $2M$ to $D$ but the text (line 114) claims it increases from $2M$ to $C$. Is that just a mistake, given that $C$ is later (line 162) defined as the number of classes?

paper_formatting_concerns.value:
This is a minor nitpick, but many metrics are only named by their abbreviations (SI-SDRi, SDRi, SA-SDR) and should be defined the first time they are named, e.g. scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio improvement (SI-SDRi), etc.

The same is true for $D$, $T'$ and $C$ in Figure 2. It is not immediately obvious what they are supposed to be from the Figure alone.

The description of Table 3 should also mention it is the SI-SDRi in dB which is reported.

final_justification.value: The provided updated experiments, particularly regarding the computational cost of the proposed architecture made me increase the rating to borderline accept.

title.value: DeepASA: An Object-Oriented Multi-Purpose Network for Auditory Scene Analysis

TLDR.value: We propose DeepASA, an object-oriented one-for-all network that mimics human auditory scene analysis to perform source separation, sound event detection, and direction-of-arrival estimation, achieving state-of-the-art performance on downstream tasks.

abstract.value: We propose DeepASA, a multi-purpose model for auditory scene analysis that performs multi-input multi-output (MIMO) source separation, dereverberation, sound event detection (SED), audio classification, and direction-of-arrival estimation (DoAE) within a unified framework. DeepASA is designed for complex auditory scenes where multiple, often similar, sound sources overlap in time and move dynamically in space. To achieve robust and consistent inference across tasks, we introduce an object-oriented processing (OOP) strategy. This approach encapsulates diverse auditory features into object-centric representations and refines them through a chain-of-inference (CoI) mechanism. The pipeline comprises a dynamic temporal kernel-based feature extractor, a transformer-based aggregator, and an object separator that yields per-object features. These features feed into multiple task-specific decoders. Our object-centric representations naturally resolve the parameter association ambiguity inherent in traditional track-wise processing. However, early-stage object separation can lead to failure in downstream ASA tasks. To address this, we implement temporal coherence matching (TCM) within the chain-of-inference, enabling multi-task fusion and iterative refinement of object features using estimated auditory parameters. We evaluate DeepASA on representative spatial audio benchmark datasets, including ASA2, MC-FUSS, and STARSS23. Experimental results show that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness in both source separation and auditory parameter estimation under diverse spatial auditory scenes. The demo video, samples and code are available at https://huggingface.co/spaces/donghoney22/DeepASA.
